name: Katong Laksa
description: Thick rice noodles drowned in a fiery santan curry broth rich with coconut milk, creamy, spicy and chilli-hot, layered with dried shrimp, cockles, fishcake and a dollop of sambal. Snipped short so you slurp the whole steaming bowl with just a spoon, Katong-style.
stall: 328 Katong Laksa, East Coast Road
notes: CHIP 2 HERO (paraphrase) + CHIP 5 (geospatial, East) — must never contain literal: spicy, coconut, milk, noodle, soup

name: Nasi Lemak
description: Fragrant rice cooked in rich coconut milk and pandan, stacked with crispy fried chicken wing, ikan bilis, peanuts, egg and a sweet-spicy sambal. Wrapped the old way for breakfast on the go.
stall: Selera Rasa Nasi Lemak, Adam Road Food Centre
notes: CHIP 2 LEXICAL DISTRACTOR — keeps literal 'coconut milk' + 'spicy'; Keyword/Naive wrongly rank this over Katong Laksa

name: Hainanese Chicken Rice
description: Silky poached chicken draped over rice cooked in chicken fat and stock, with chilli-ginger sauce and dark soy. A national obsession judged on the sheen of the bird and the perfume of the rice.
stall: Tian Tian Hainanese Chicken Rice, Maxwell Food Centre
notes: CHIP 1 HERO — exact multi-word name, all 4 columns agree

name: Sambal Stingray
description: A whole stingray wing — meaty, flaky fish — smothered in pungent sambal belacan and char-grilled until the edges blister, served sizzling with cincalok and calamansi. Smoky, fiery and best torn apart while scalding hot.
stall: Chomp Chomp BBQ, Chomp Chomp Food Centre

name: Otah
description: Spiced mackerel fish mousse blended with santan and rempah, pressed flat and char-grilled inside a coconut-frond parcel until custardy and smoky. Eaten straight off the charcoal or tucked into bread.
stall: Muar Traditional Otah, East Coast Lagoon Food Village

name: Thosai
description: A crisp, lacy fermented rice-and-lentil crepe served on a banana leaf with coconut chutney, tomato chutney and sambar. Order it plain, masala-stuffed or paper-thin for a light, tangy South Indian breakfast.
stall: MTR-style Dosa Corner, Tekka Centre

name: Banana Leaf Rice
description: Steamed rice heaped onto a fresh banana leaf and ringed with vegetable curries, rasam, papadum and pickles, refilled generously as you eat. Fold the leaf towards you when done to compliment the kitchen.
stall: Ananda Curry House, Tekka Centre
notes: CHIP 3 candidate answer (pure concept, rainy-day) — semantic surfaces this on 'warm and filling' queries

name: Mee Soto
description: A comforting halal soup: springy yellow noodles plunged into a rich, spice-heavy chicken broth perfumed with lemongrass and galangal, crowned with shredded ayam, bergedil and fiery sambal kicap. Worth every minute of the interchange queue.
stall: Inspirasi, Bedok Interchange Hawker Centre
notes: CHIP 5 (geospatial, East/Bedok) — halal + Bedok + broth vocabulary

name: Bak Chor Mee
description: Fengshan's famous minced pork noodle soup: mee pok in a pork-bone broth loaded with minced pork, liver, meatballs and crispy lard, sharpened with vinegar and chilli. Queues at Bedok 85 run deep into the night.
stall: Xing Ji Rou Cuo Mian, Bedok 85 Fengshan Centre
notes: CHIP 5 (geospatial, East/Bedok) — pork so not halal, but a strong 'spicy noodle soup' semantic match

name: Prawn Mee
description: Yellow mee and bee hoon in an intensely savoury stock coaxed from wok-roasted prawn heads and pork bones, topped with prawns, pork ribs and fried shallots. Deep, sweet crustacean flavour in every slurp.
stall: Beach Road Prawn Mee, East Coast Road
notes: CHIP 5 (geospatial, East Coast) — great noodle-soup concept, pork stock so not halal

name: Fish Head Curry
description: A whole red snapper head simmered in a bubbling tamarind-tinged curry with okra, brinjal and tomatoes, South Indian style. The cheek meat is the prize; the gravy demands rice or bread for mopping.
stall: Gayatri Curry Corner, Tekka Centre

name: Char Kway Teow
description: Flat rice ribbons and yellow mee seared in pork lard over ferocious heat with dark soy, cockles, lap cheong and egg, kissed by wok hei. Smoky, sweet-savoury and gloriously unapologetic.
stall: Outram Park Fried Kway Teow, Hong Lim Food Centre

name: Hokkien Mee
description: Yellow mee and thick bee hoon braised in a rich prawn-and-pork stock until every strand drinks it up, finished with prawns, sotong, lard croutons, sambal and a squeeze of lime.
stall: Geylang Lor 29 Fried Hokkien Mee, Geylang

name: Wanton Mee
description: Springy egg noodles tossed in a sweet-savoury sauce with char siew slices, leafy greens and plump pork-and-prawn dumplings on the side. Comes dry with chilli or drenched in light broth.
stall: Fei Fei Wanton Mee, Joo Chiat Place

name: Bak Kut Teh
description: Meaty pork ribs simmered in a peppery, garlicky broth until spoon-tender, refilled endlessly and chased with you tiao and hot tea. The ultimate warming bowl on a grey, drizzly evening.
stall: Ya Hua Bak Kut Teh, Outram
notes: CHIP 3 candidate — rainy-day comfort vocabulary, but over $5 (talking point)

name: Century Egg Pork Porridge
description: Silky rice congee simmered to a cloud, laced with tender pork slivers, century egg, ginger and crispy shallots. Soothing, warming comfort food made for gloomy rainy afternoons and fragile mornings alike.
stall: Zhen Zhen Porridge, Maxwell Food Centre
notes: CHIP 3 HERO (pure concept, rainy-day) — comfort + rainy vocabulary, under $5

name: Roti Prata
description: Ghee-laminated dough flipped and stretched paper-thin, griddled until shatteringly crisp outside and chewy within, then dunked into fish or mutton curry. Order it plain, egg, or audaciously with cheese.
stall: Mr and Mrs Mohgan's Super Crispy Roti Prata, Joo Chiat

name: Mee Goreng
description: Mamak-style yellow mee wok-fried with tomato, potato, egg, taupok and a fiery red chilli paste, tangy and pedas in equal measure. An Indian-Muslim classic that pairs dangerously well with teh tarik.
stall: Haji Kadir Mee Goreng, Tekka Centre

name: Mee Rebus
description: Yellow mee blanketed in a thick, sweet-savoury gravy of sweet potato, dried shrimp and spices, finished with egg, green chilli, taukwa and a squeeze of calamansi. Javanese-rooted and deeply comforting.
stall: Afandi Hawa & Family Mee Rebus, Geylang Serai Market
notes: CHIP 4 HERO (clean win / Hybrid hero) — 'javanese noodles in sweet potato gravy': Keyword and Naive both narrowly misrank Curry Chicken Noodles above this; Semantic and RRF correctly lead with Mee Rebus

name: Sup Tulang
description: Mutton leg bones stewed in a shocking-red, sweet-spiced tomato gravy until the marrow slides free — sucked straight from the bone or scooped with baguette. A gloriously messy Indian-Muslim supper ritual.
stall: Haji M. Abdul Rajak, Golden Mile Food Centre

name: Chendol
description: A snow-capped mound of shaved ice drowned in smoky gula melaka and creamy santan, hiding chewy pandan jellies, red beans and attap chee below. Sweet, cooling salvation on a sweltering afternoon.
stall: Old Amoy Chendol, Chinatown Complex

name: Kaya Toast Set
description: Charcoal-grilled bread sandwiching cold butter and fragrant pandan-egg kaya, served with wobbly soft-boiled eggs for dipping and a thick kopi. The definitive old-school Singapore breakfast ritual.
stall: Tong Ah Eating House, Keong Saik Road

name: Chicken Satay
description: Turmeric-marinated chicken skewers fanned over charcoal until charred and juicy, served with chunky peanut sauce, ketupat, cucumber and raw onion. Smoke, sweetness and spice on a stick.
stall: Haron Satay, Lau Pa Sat Satay Street

name: Nasi Briyani
description: Long-grain basmati steamed with ghee, saffron and whole spices, buried under a fall-apart chicken or mutton curry with achar and papadum. Fragrant, festive and unapologetically generous.
stall: Allauddin's Briyani, Tekka Centre

name: Mutton Murtabak
description: Prata dough folded around spiced minced mutton, onion and egg, griddled golden and cut into hefty squares, served with curry and pickled onions. A crisp-edged, savoury Indian-Muslim heavyweight.
stall: Geylang Serai Famous Murtabak, Geylang Serai Market

name: Mala Xiang Guo
description: Pick-your-own ingredients stir-fried in a numbing, tongue-tingling Sichuan mala sauce heavy with dried chillies and peppercorns. Choose xiao la if you value your tastebuds; da la if you don't.
stall: Ri Ri Hong Mala Xiang Guo, People's Park Complex

name: Ban Mian
description: Hand-torn dough noodles in a light anchovy-and-pork broth with minced pork, sayur manis, a cracked egg and crispy ikan bilis. Homely, slippery and quietly addictive on a cold day.
stall: L32 Handmade Noodles, Geylang Lor 32

name: Curry Puff
description: A flaky golden pastry pocket stuffed with curried potato, chicken and a wedge of hard-boiled egg, fried to a blistered crisp. Singapore's favourite teatime snack since forever.
stall: Wang Wang Crispy Curry Puff, Old Airport Road Food Centre

name: Teh Tarik
description: Strong black tea and condensed milk pulled between two mugs in long theatrical arcs until frothy, silky and just short of scalding. The sweet, milky heartbeat of every mamak stall.
stall: Ar Rahman Cafe, Tekka Centre

name: Chilli Crab
description: Whole mud crab wok-tossed in a sweet-savoury chilli-tomato gravy thickened with egg ribbons, mopped up with golden fried mantou buns. Messy, celebratory and worth every shell-cracked knuckle.
stall: East Coast Seafood Corner, East Coast Lagoon Food Village
